body.heading: No is a complete sentence — but it can wear a coat
paragraphs: You do not owe anyone a long trial in which your reasons are cross-examined. Still, a small coat of warmth helps: “I can’t this time, but thank you for asking,” costs nothing and changes how the no lands.
Avoid fake excuses. They have a way of being discovered, and then the no and the dishonesty both need forgiving.

body.heading: Say what you can do
paragraphs: If you want to help but cannot do the thing asked, name the smaller thing you can do. “I can’t lend the car, but I can drive you on Saturday.” A clear alternative turns a closed door into a side window.
If there is nothing you can offer, that is allowed too. A plain no, kindly said, is not a failure of friendship.

body.heading: Hold it gently and firmly
paragraphs: Sometimes a no needs repeating, word for word, without growing louder or sharper: “I understand it’s disappointing. I still can’t.” Repetition is not rudeness; it is steadiness.
People who respect you may be disappointed, but they will not punish you for a boundary. That difference tells you a great deal.

takeaway: Keep your no short, honest, and warm — and let it stand without a court case.
